summary:
Martinique stands under France's national framework. Article 73 of the Constitution applies French law to the department in full, so identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime operate here as in the metropole. Same-sex conduct has been decriminalised since 1815, the 2013 marriage-equality law applies, and gender-marker change is available through the simplified judicial route introduced by the state's 2016-17 reforms.

Discrimination protection rests on several instruments that reach the island directly. Goods and services have been covered since Law No. 2001-1066 (Penal Code articles 225-1 and 225-2), employment since Labour Code article L1132-1 in 2008, and discrimination on grounds of gender identity since Article 4 of the 2012 sexual-harassment law, where the wording 'sexual identity' was replaced by 'gender identity' in 2016. Nothing in the criminal law criminalises being trans.

Detention is the sharp exception. Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code requires that detainees be placed in facilities matching the gender marker on their identity documents, so placement follows the marker rather than anatomy. In practice most trans women are therefore held in all-male facilities, where other detainees threaten them; a BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 records detainees telling trans women 'we don't want any women here'. The French prison framework governs Martinique's establishments as French law, and this pattern of placement and threat reaches them.

The CGLPL, France's detention-places watchdog, issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 finding 'the persistence of serious violations' of the fundamental rights of transgender detainees across all French places of deprivation of liberty. The finding rests on referrals received since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons and on inspections at which eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed, and it makes recommendations on placement, isolation, safety and staff training. Because the opinion addresses French establishments as a category, its findings bind the department's prisons too.

Community infrastructure on the island is real but small. JM Concept 972 is a Martinique lesbian, gay, bi and trans network providing information, meetings and services, and running private parties and garden parties supported by gay-friendly heterosexual supporters, with dated events listed for 4 July, 15 August and 5 September 2025.
tangentialFactors:
The island's legal position is metropolitan in almost every respect, so the divergence a trans visitor should expect is concentrated in custodial settings rather than in entry, documentation, marriage or public-space law. Where the sources describe risk, they describe it inside detention.

The CGLPL opinion is a national finding drawn from sites in France itself; it establishes the standard of treatment French establishments are held to, and it is the most substantial official admission of harm to trans detainees in the French system.

Comparison with the surrounding legal picture is unhelpful for visitors worried about criminal liability: the conduct at issue has not been an offence on the island for two centuries, and the contemporary dispute concerns the adequacy of protection and custodial treatment rather than legality.
localsOnly:
Residents can rely on the same statutory protections as in the metropole: Penal Code articles 225-1 and 225-2 for goods and services since Law No. 2001-1066, Labour Code article L1132-1 for employment since 2008, and Article 4 of the 2012 sexual-harassment law for gender identity since the 2016 wording change.

Local support is anchored by JM Concept 972, a lesbian, gay, bi and trans network running information, meetings and services alongside private and garden parties, with a 2025 calendar that includes 4 July, 15 August and 5 September. Rights in Exile (AsyLex) maintains a Martinique resource page listing local support organisations, relevant case law and country-of-origin experts.

For residents entering the prison system, placement follows the gender marker on the identity document under Article D248, and the CGLPL's recommendations on placement, isolation, safety and staff training form part of the oversight record they can invoke.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the sources give no inspection or incident data specific to Martinique's own prisons. The CGLPL opinion is national in scope and the sites it names for interviews are metropolitan, so its application to the island's establishments follows from their status as French places of deprivation of liberty rather than from a documented local inspection.

Unresolved: no source in the inventory records enforcement outcomes for gender-identity discrimination claims brought on the island, nor local court decisions on gender-marker change here.

Unresolved: the inventory does not state whether the CGLPL's recommendations on placement, isolation, safety and staff training have been implemented in Martinique's facilities.
